title: Where God Weeps
hookLine: he taught that God weeps in an inner chamber alongside His people (Chagigah 5b)
carry: in the inner room, God weeps with us
tomorrow: what do you do with something old that still matters?

lines: CRYING IN THE CAR, IN THE DRIVEWAY.
cards: Some people cry in the car, in the driveway, before walking into the house, so nobody inside has to see. The Talmud says God has a place like that.
In tractate Chagigah the rabbis read a line of Jeremiah, where God's soul weeps in secret places, and they say: God has a place called mistarim, the hidden places, and there He weeps.
So that's where God goes: somewhere hidden, on the inside.

teach.b: The Talmud even notices a problem. Another verse says strength and gladness are in God's place. How can both be true?
Its answer: there are inner rooms and outer rooms. In the outer rooms, strength and gladness. In the inner rooms, weeping.
Rabbi Shapira, in the ghetto, took this passage and made it a door.
God isn't far off, watching His people suffer; God weeps with them, in the inner room.
And a person who comes into that room to weep with God, he teaches, finds something there: strength. You aren't crying alone, and neither is God. That's the life part of today.
When someone you love is hurting, the instinct is to fix it, to find the perfect sentence, to point at the bright side. The inner-room teaching offers a different job: go in and sit there.
Weep with them, if weeping is what's happening. Jewish mourning custom carries the same wisdom.

teach.h: SIT, AND LET THE MOURNER SPEAK.
teach.b: When people visit a house of mourning during shiva, the custom is to sit quietly and let the mourner speak first.

teach.h: IN THE INNER ROOM, GOD WEEPS WITH US.
teach.b: Nobody has to arrive with the answer. Being in the room is the answer. And the passage offers something to the one grieving, too.
Tears aren't a sign that God has gone. In the Talmud's picture, the room where the tears are is where God is.

how: In Jewish mourning, family members sit shiva for a week after a burial, and visitors come to sit with them, often waiting for the mourner to speak first and offering a traditional word of comfort as they leave.

games.q: a coworker's dog died, and the team chat fills up with 'at least he had a good life!' you want to reach out to her. what does the inner room suggest?
o: a short note: i'm so sorry. i'm here, no need to reply.
a few reasons it was for the best, to help her move on.
nothing yet; give it a week before anyone brings it up.
games.why: the inner-room teaching isn't about fixing grief. it's about coming in and sitting with it, the way God weeps with us.

practice: Bring to mind someone carrying something heavy right now, or a sorrow of your own. Put a hand on your heart and say their name softly, out loud, or your own.
For the sit, don't try to fix anything; just stay in the room with it, the way the Talmud pictures God staying in the inner room.

wordCard.voice: God weeps with us: from Chagigah 5b, God weeping in the hidden places, read by Rabbi Shapira as God beside His people in their grief.

orig.note: Hebrew: hidden places; in Chagigah 5b, where God weeps.

carryVoice: Something to hold: in the inner room, god weeps with us, so sitting with someone's grief is holy work, not a failure to fix it. Gently, until tomorrow.
